  • 0.5 is a good balance — your intuition holds. Moving from 0.4 to 0.5 cuts wasted contacts from 31 to 20 per 100 for a drop in recall from 0.74 to 0.60.
    • 

  • Beyond 0.5 the returns shrink. Going from 0.5 to 0.6 avoids 53 wasted contacts but also loses 63 successful ones — almost a one-for-one swap. From 0.6 upwards precision barely improves (0.86 → 0.87 → 0.89) while recall keeps collapsing. The precision–recall chart shows the same "knee" around 0.5–0.6.
    • 

  • A low cut-off is not an option for us. At 0.3 we would contact 70 % of all clients, with 42 wasted contacts per 100 — which defeats the purpose of a limited-capacity campaign.
    • 



Capacity rule. If the contact centre can only handle a fixed number of clients, ignore the cut-off and contact the top K. From the gains table: the top 10 % of clients have a 92 % hit rate, the top 30 % 85 %, the top 50 % 70 %, against 48 % when contacting at random.


Our answer¶
    

  • Minimise false positives — but not at any price. Every false positive wastes a scarce contact, so we judge the model by its precision. Because precision alone can be gamed by contacting only a handful of sure clients, we always read it together with recall / volume.
    • 

  • Keep 0.5 as the default operating point (precision 0.80, recall 0.60, ≈ 20 wasted contacts per 100). It is where the trade-off flattens out. The Streamlit app has a cut-off slider and a "maximum clients to contact" box so the team can move along this curve when the budget changes.
    • 

  • Note on an earlier version of this analysis. An earlier draft argued for a cut-off of 0.30–0.35. That reasoning assumed the bank could contact as many clients as it liked and only compared the value of a deposit with the cost of a call. Under the capacity and cost-sustainability limits described in §1, that assumption no longer holds, and the conclusion flips towards precision.
    • 























13. Over- and underfitting checks¶
A model can fail in two opposite ways:







Underfitting (high bias)
Overfitting (high variance)






What happens
The model is too simple to capture the pattern
The model memorises the training data, noise included




Training score
Low
Very high




Validation / test score
Low (about the same as training)
Much lower than training




Typical cause
Too few features, too-simple model, too much regularisation
Too-flexible model, too little data, too little regularisation




Typical cure
More expressive model or better features
Simpler model, more regularisation, more data, early stopping






The key diagnostic is the gap between the training score and the validation score. We look at it in three ways: a train/CV/test table, learning curves, and validation curves.


13.1 Train vs cross-validation vs test score — every model¶
A big gap between the training AUC and the CV AUC is the classic symptom of overfitting. We also compare CV with test: if they disagree strongly, the model (or our tuning) has been over-optimistic.


















In [47]:






# (auc_on() was defined in section 12)
rows = []
for name in comparison.index:
    if name.startswith("Baseline"):
        continue                                                              # baselines have nothing to overfit
    rows.append({"model": name,
                 "train_auc": auc_on(name, X_train, y_train),                 # score on data the model has SEEN
                 "cv_auc": comparison.loc[name, "cv_auc_mean"],               # score on held-out folds
                 "test_auc": comparison.loc[name, "test_roc_auc"]})           # score on the untouched test set
fit_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model")
fit_table["train_minus_cv"] = fit_table["train_auc"] - fit_table["cv_auc"]    # the overfitting gap

best_cv = fit_table["cv_auc"].max()
def diagnose(row):
    # Simple rules of thumb (thresholds are judgement calls, not laws)
    if row["train_minus_cv"] > 0.10:
        return "overfitting"
    if row["train_minus_cv"] > 0.05:
        return "mild overfitting"
    if row["cv_auc"] < best_cv - 0.01:
        return "possible underfitting"                                        # small gap, but also clearly lower than the best model
    return "well balanced"
fit_table["diagnosis"] = fit_table.apply(diagnose, axis=1)
display(fit_table.sort_values("train_minus_cv", ascending=False).style.format(
    {"train_auc": "{:.3f}", "cv_auc": "{:.3f}", "test_auc": "{:.3f}", "train_minus_cv": "{:+.3f}"}))

# Visual: train (grey) vs CV (blue) vs test (orange). A long grey tail = memorisation.
plot_df = fit_table.sort_values("cv_auc")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.5))
y_pos = np.arange(len(plot_df))
ax.barh(y_pos + 0.27, plot_df["train_auc"], height=0.26, color="#8c9aa8", label="Train")
ax.barh(y_pos, plot_df["cv_auc"], height=0.26, color="#2a6f97", label="Cross-validation")
ax.barh(y_pos - 0.27, plot_df["test_auc"], height=0.26, color=COLORS["yes"], label="Test")
ax.set_yticks(y_pos); ax.set_yticklabels(plot_df.index); ax.set_xlim(0.6, 1.0)
ax.set_xlabel("ROC-AUC"); ax.set_title("Train vs CV vs test — a gap between grey and blue means overfitting"); ax.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

13.2 Learning curves¶
A learning curve retrains the model on growing slices of the training data and plots training vs validation score. It tells us what would help:


    

  • Both curves flat and close together at a low score → underfitting; more data will not help, a richer model or better features might.
    • 

  • A big gap that is slowly closing → overfitting; more data or more regularisation should help.
    • 

  • Validation curve still rising at 100 % of the data → more data would help.
    • 



















In [48]:






curve_models = ["Logistic Regression", "Random Forest", "XGBoost"]            # one simple, one very flexible, one boosted model
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.3), sharey=True)
for ax, name in zip(axes, curve_models):
    sizes, train_scores, valid_scores = learning_curve(
        clone(fitted[name]),                                                  # clone = fresh copy with the same tuned settings
        X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc",
        train_sizes=np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 6), n_jobs=-1, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
    for scores, label, colour in [(train_scores, "Training", "#8c9aa8"), (valid_scores, "Validation (CV)", COLORS["yes"])]:
        ax.plot(sizes, scores.mean(axis=1), "o-", color=colour, label=label)
        ax.fill_between(sizes, scores.mean(axis=1) - scores.std(axis=1), scores.mean(axis=1) + scores.std(axis=1), color=colour, alpha=0.15)
    ax.set_title(name); ax.set_xlabel("Training-set size"); ax.grid(True)
axes[0].set_ylabel("ROC-AUC"); axes[0].legend(loc="center right")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
















































13.3 Validation curves — finding the right complexity¶
A validation curve varies one complexity setting and plots training vs validation score. As complexity grows, training keeps improving, but validation peaks and then falls: the peak is the sweet spot, to its left we underfit, to its right we overfit.


We use two classic examples: the depth of a decision tree, and the number of boosting rounds for XGBoost.


















In [49]:






fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.3))

# ---- (a) Decision tree depth ----
depths = list(range(1, 17))
tree_pipe = Pipeline([("prep", make_preprocessor(False)), ("model", DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE))])
train_scores, valid_scores = validation_curve(tree_pipe, X_train, y_train, param_name="model__max_depth", param_range=depths,
                                              cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1)

# ---- (b) Number of boosting rounds for XGBoost (other settings = the tuned ones) ----
rounds = [25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1200]
xgb_train_scores, xgb_valid_scores = validation_curve(clone(fitted["XGBoost"]), X_train, y_train, param_name="model__n_estimators",
                                                      param_range=rounds, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1)

for ax, x_values, tr, va, title, xlabel in [
        (axes[0], depths, train_scores, valid_scores, "Decision tree", "max_depth  (simple  →  complex)"),
        (axes[1], rounds, xgb_train_scores, xgb_valid_scores, "XGBoost", "n_estimators  (simple  →  complex)")]:
    ax.plot(x_values, tr.mean(axis=1), "o-", color="#8c9aa8", label="Training")
    ax.plot(x_values, va.mean(axis=1), "o-", color=COLORS["yes"], label="Validation (CV)")
    ax.fill_between(x_values, va.mean(axis=1) - va.std(axis=1), va.mean(axis=1) + va.std(axis=1), color=COLORS["yes"], alpha=0.15)
    best_x = x_values[int(np.argmax(va.mean(axis=1)))]                        # the setting with the best validation score
    ax.axvline(best_x, color="black", ls="--", lw=1, label=f"best validation = {best_x}")
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel(xlabel); ax.set_ylabel("ROC-AUC"); ax.legend(loc="center right"); ax.grid(True)
axes[1].set_xscale("log")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
















































What the diagnostics say¶
1. No model is badly overfit, and the test set was not "burnt". The largest train-minus-CV gap is +0.095 (YDF), below our 0.10 "overfitting" threshold. For every model the test AUC is equal to or slightly higher than the CV AUC, so our tuning did not make the CV scores over-optimistic.


2. Three models overfit mildly — the ones with the deepest, least-regularised trees:


    

  • YDF (train 0.877 vs CV 0.781, gap +0.095), Random forest (0.856 vs 0.779, +0.077), Decision tree (0.803 vs 0.742, +0.061).
    • 

  • They memorise some noise, but this does not cost them validation accuracy: they tie with the better-regularised boosters.
    • 



3. The tuned boosters are the best balanced (gaps +0.028 to +0.047). Note that the two Optuna models reach the same validation score as their random-search twins with the smallest gaps (+0.033 and +0.028): Optuna found more conservative trees (high gamma, 50 % row sampling) for no loss of accuracy — that is exactly why the LightGBM (Optuna) model is the one selected as best in §12 and deployed in §15.


4. Logistic regression is bias-limited (mild underfitting). Its train AUC (0.772) is almost the same as its CV AUC (0.765): no overfitting, but also no room to improve. The learning curve confirms it — both lines are flat and sit on top of each other, so more data will not help; the limit is the straight-line structure of the model, even with our engineered features. It is still only ~0.016 AUC behind the boosters, so little is lost.


5. Learning curves. For the random forest the gap between the curves stays large and constant (~0.08) while validation AUC creeps upward: more data would help a little. For XGBoost the gap narrows as data grows (training falls from 0.86 to 0.82, validation rises from 0.72 to 0.78) and validation is still rising at 100 % — more data would probably still help, with slowing returns.


6. Validation curves show the textbook shapes.


    

  • Decision tree: validation AUC peaks at depth ≈ 7 (CV ≈ 0.73). Left of that it underfits; beyond it, training AUC keeps soaring (0.92 at depth 16) while validation falls to 0.68 — clear overfitting.
    • 

  • XGBoost: validation AUC is highest around 400 rounds (≈ 0.78) and drifts down slightly with many more (0.773 at 1 200) while training AUC keeps climbing. Between about 200 and 400 rounds the curve is flat within its error band.
    • 



Bottom line: we are not hiding an overfit model, and the remaining gaps are small. Since the validation curves have flattened, further gains would come from more data or better features, not from more tuning. (The "diagnosis" thresholds in the table are rules of thumb, not laws.)






















14. Explainable AI (XAI) & feature importance¶
A model that scores well but cannot be explained is hard to trust and hard to act on — and a campaign manager will want to know why a client was flagged as a prospect.


From here on we analyse only two models: our best model (selected in §12) and Google's YDF. We do not repeat the analysis for every model we trained.






Method
Question it answers
Scope






Permutation importance
"If I scramble this feature, how much worse does the model get?"
Global, any model




SHAP values
"How much did each feature push this client's prediction up or down?"
Global + individual (best model)




Partial dependence (PDP)
"On average, how does the prediction change as this feature changes?"
Global (best model)




Built-in importance
The model's own view of itself
Model-specific (YDF)






14.1 Permutation importance (model-agnostic, computed on the test set)¶
Idea: take the test set, shuffle one column so it becomes meaningless noise, and see how much the AUC drops. A big drop = the model relied on that column. We write it by hand (it is only a few lines) so it works for both of our models, including YDF.


















In [50]:






def permutation_importance_auc(predict_fn, X, y, n_repeats=10, seed=RANDOM_STATE):
    """For each feature: shuffle it `n_repeats` times and record the average drop in ROC-AUC (bigger drop = more important)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    baseline_auc = roc_auc_score(y, predict_fn(X))                 # score with nothing shuffled
    importance = {}
    for col in X.columns:
        drops = []
        for _ in range(n_repeats):
            X_shuffled = X.copy()
            X_shuffled[col] = rng.permutation(X_shuffled[col].to_numpy())   # shuffle only this column
            drops.append(baseline_auc - roc_auc_score(y, predict_fn(X_shuffled)))
        importance[col] = np.mean(drops)
    return pd.Series(importance).sort_values(ascending=False)

# Two models, one common yardstick
perm = pd.DataFrame({
    best_name: permutation_importance_auc(lambda d: fitted[best_name].predict_proba(d)[:, 1], X_test, y_test),
    "YDF (Google)": permutation_importance_auc(lambda d: ydf_model.predict(d), X_test, y_test),
})
perm = perm.loc[perm.mean(axis=1).sort_values(ascending=False).index]     # order by average importance

ax = perm.plot.barh(figsize=(9, 6), width=0.8, color=[COLORS["yes"], "#2a6f97"])
ax.invert_yaxis()                                                          # most important at the top
ax.set_xlabel("Drop in test ROC-AUC when the feature is shuffled")
ax.set_title("Permutation importance — best model vs YDF")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
display(perm.head(10).round(4))                                            # the same numbers as a table

# Do the two models agree on which features matter most?
rank_agreement = perm.corr(method="spearman").iloc[0, 1]
print(f"Spearman rank correlation between the two importance rankings: {rank_agreement:.2f}  (1 = identical order)")

14.2 SHAP — explaining the best model¶
SHAP borrows an idea from game theory: treat the features as team members and fairly split the credit for the prediction among them. For each client, SHAP gives each feature a number:


    

  • positive (→ right) = pushed the prediction towards yes
    • 

  • negative (← left) = pushed it towards no
    • 



The numbers are in "log-odds" units (the model's internal scale). Bigger magnitude = bigger influence.


We explain the model on the test set (data it has not trained on), using the fast tree-specific explainer.


















In [51]:






best_pipeline = fitted[best_name]
X_test_encoded = best_pipeline.named_steps["prep"].transform(X_test)      # the table exactly as the model sees it (one-hot columns etc.)
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(best_pipeline.named_steps["model"])        # explainer for tree models
shap_values = explainer(X_test_encoded)                                   # one SHAP number per client per feature
if shap_values.values.ndim == 3:                                          # some versions return one slice per class: keep "yes"
    shap_values = shap_values[..., 1]
print("SHAP matrix shape (clients x features):", shap_values.values.shape)

























SHAP matrix shape (clients x features): (1561, 47)





















In [52]:






# Global view 1: average absolute impact per feature (a "bar" importance chart)
shap.plots.bar(shap_values, max_display=15, show=False)
plt.title("Mean |SHAP value| — which features move predictions the most"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# The same ranking as a table: mean absolute SHAP value per encoded column
mean_abs_shap = pd.Series(np.abs(shap_values.values).mean(axis=0), index=X_test_encoded.columns).sort_values(ascending=False)
display(mean_abs_shap.head(10).to_frame("mean_abs_shap"))

# One-hot columns split a feature over many bars (month -> 12 bars). Adding them back together gives one number per ORIGINAL feature.
from bank_inference import group_shap
grouped = group_shap(shap_values, X_test_encoded.columns)
display(grouped.abs().mean().sort_values(ascending=False).head(10).to_frame("mean_abs_shap (grouped by original feature)"))

# Direction of the effect: average SHAP value when a one-hot column is ON (1). Positive = pushes towards yes.
direction = {}
for col in ["poutcome_success", "month_may", "month_mar", "month_oct", "contact_unknown", "housing_no", "was_contacted_before"]:
    is_on = X_test_encoded[col].to_numpy() == 1
    direction[col] = shap_values.values[is_on, list(X_test_encoded.columns).index(col)].mean()
display(pd.Series(direction).to_frame("avg_shap_when_ON"))

# Global view 2: the "beeswarm". Each dot is ONE client.
#  x-position  = how much this feature pushed that client's prediction (right = towards yes)
#  colour      = the feature's value for that client (red = high, blue = low)
shap.plots.beeswarm(shap_values, max_display=15, show=False)
plt.title("SHAP beeswarm — direction and size of each feature's effect"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
















































How to read the beeswarm. For a one-hot column such as poutcome_success, red means "1 = the client is in this category". If the red dots sit far to the right, then being in that category strongly pushes towards yes. For numeric features, such as age or balance_slog, the colour gradient shows high vs low values.

# Individual explanations: why did the model score THESE two clients the way it did?

most_likely_no = int(np.argmin(proba_best))        # the client the model is MOST sure will say no

    shap.plots.waterfall(shap_values[idx], max_display=10, show=False)    # step-by-step: baseline -> prediction

14.3 Partial dependence plots (PDP)¶
SHAP explains individual predictions; a partial dependence plot shows the average predicted probability as one feature varies and everything else is left as observed. It answers "what happens to the prediction if we change only this?"


















In [56]:






# scikit-learn refuses whole-number (int) columns in PDPs, so we use a copy where numeric columns are decimals (floats)
X_test_pdp = X_test.copy()
X_test_pdp[NUMERIC_FEATURES] = X_test_pdp[NUMERIC_FEATURES].astype(float)

# (We skip pdays_clean here: 74 % of its values are missing, which scikit-learn's PDP cannot handle.)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.8))
PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(
    best_pipeline, X_test_pdp, features=["age", "balance_slog", "campaign_log"],
    ax=ax, kind="average",                              # the average effect across all clients
)
plt.suptitle(f"Partial dependence — {best_name}", y=1.03); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# categorical features need to be flagged with categorical_features
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 4))
PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(
    best_pipeline, X_test_pdp, features=["poutcome", "month"], categorical_features=["poutcome", "month"], ax=ax)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



























































14.4 YDF's own view¶
YDF can report importance from the structure of its own trees. SUM_SCORE is the total split-quality gain a feature contributed across all trees. It is a different lens from permutation importance (it measures how much the trees used a feature, not how much the score drops without it).


















In [57]:






ydf_importance = pd.DataFrame(ydf_model.variable_importances()["SUM_SCORE"], columns=["importance", "feature"])
ydf_importance = ydf_importance.set_index("feature")["importance"].sort_values()
ydf_importance.plot.barh(figsize=(7, 5), color="#2a6f97")
plt.xlabel("SUM_SCORE (total split gain)"); plt.title("YDF built-in variable importance"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
















































14.5 What the explanations say¶
We analysed two models: our best model (LightGBM (Optuna)) and YDF. They tell a consistent story.


    

  1. Both models agree on what matters. In permutation importance (grouped by original column) the top three are the same for both: contact, month and poutcome (best model: 0.075, 0.058, 0.044; YDF: 0.052, 0.080, 0.025), followed by balance_slog. The Spearman rank correlation between the two full rankings is 0.86. Two different algorithms pointing to the same features makes the finding trustworthy.
    2. 

  2. Previous success is the single strongest push. In SHAP, poutcome_success has the largest mean impact of any encoded column (0.31) and, when "on", adds about +1.5 log-odds — roughly 4.4× higher odds of yes. This matches the EDA (91 % of previously-successful clients subscribe again).
    3. 

  3. contact is the most influential feature once its one-hot columns are added together (grouped SHAP 0.38). contact = unknown pulls predictions down by about 0.5 log-odds (≈ 0.6× the odds); cellular pushes up. Remember from §6.1 that "unknown" is concentrated in May–June (MAR), so the model partly reads how the data was recorded. It stays valid only if future data is logged the same way.
    4. 

  4. Some months push strongly up (March +1.0, October +0.7 log-odds on average), and the partial-dependence plot shows the same: highest in March (≈ 0.73), October (≈ 0.68) and June (≈ 0.65), lowest in January (≈ 0.40) and November (≈ 0.42). One-hot encoding spreads month over 12 bars, so grouped by original feature (0.29) it ranks third in SHAP. month is the last contact month — see the limitations.
    5. 

  5. Balance matters moderately. The partial dependence is flat (~0.43) for low and negative balances, then climbs to ~0.52 for the highest balances.
    6. 

  6. Age is a U-shape, not a straight line. The partial dependence jumps from ≈ 0.46 to ≈ 0.64 at age 60, and the youngest clients (≈ 0.57) sit above the middle-aged. SHAP gives age a visible weight (0.13) while permutation importance gives it almost none, because age and age_group carry the same information (VIF in §8.1) — shuffle one and the model still has the other.
    7. 

  7. Housing loan holders are less likely to subscribe (housing_no adds about +0.1 log-odds); loan has a small negative effect.
    8. 

  8. More contacts in the campaign → lower chance of yes. The partial dependence of campaign_log falls from ≈ 0.49 to ≈ 0.30, with a sharp drop beyond roughly 11 contacts (log value ≈ 2.5): the classic "client is not interested, stop calling" pattern. But campaign is only known after the contacts were made.
    9. 



Reading this as a campaign manager. The model favours clients who: said yes before, are reachable by a recorded cellular contact, are approached in the historically better months, have a healthy balance, are under 30 or over 60, and have no housing loan.






















15. Saving the best model and deploying it in Streamlit¶
A model that lives only in a notebook cannot help the campaign team. In this section we package the best model so that anybody can use it through a small web app.


What "deployable" requires¶
    

  1. One object that does everything: raw client record → feature engineering → preprocessing → model. Until now, feature engineering lived outside the scikit-learn Pipeline. We now put it inside (using FunctionTransformer), so the app only has to pass in the 10 raw columns.
    2. 

  2. Same code in the notebook and the app. The feature-engineering function was written to bank_features.py in §7, so the app imports exactly the same function.
    3. 

  3. Trustworthy packaging. We first check that the packaged pipeline reproduces the test score we evaluated, then re-fit it on all the data (the learning curves in §13 showed more data still helps a little), then save it.
    4. 



The Parquet file¶
Parquet is a table format, so it cannot hold a model directly. We store the model as a binary column in a one-row Parquet file, next to readable columns (model name, metrics, feature list, library versions). We also save a standard .joblib copy.




⚠️ Security note: the model inside the Parquet file is a Python pickle. Loading a pickle can run code, so only load model files you created yourself (never from an unknown source).




















In [58]:






import joblib, sklearn, xgboost, lightgbm
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer
from bank_features import RAW_FEATURES
from bank_inference import save_model_parquet, load_model_parquet

raw_train = df.loc[X_train.index, RAW_FEATURES]            # the same training customers as before, but as RAW columns
raw_test = df.loc[X_test.index, RAW_FEATURES]

def build_deploy_pipeline():
    """raw client record -> feature engineering -> preprocessing -> tuned model (a fresh, unfitted copy)."""
    return Pipeline([
        ("features", FunctionTransformer(engineer_features)),                       # our function from bank_features.py
        ("prep", make_preprocessor(False)),                                         # impute + one-hot, exactly as in training
        ("model", clone(fitted[best_name].named_steps["model"])),                   # the best model with its tuned settings
    ])

# ---- Step 1: integrity check. Fit on TRAIN only: do we reproduce the test score we evaluated in section 12? ----
check_pipeline = build_deploy_pipeline().fit(raw_train, y_train)
check_proba = check_pipeline.predict_proba(raw_test)[:, 1]
print("Test AUC of the packaged pipeline :", round(roc_auc_score(y_test, check_proba), 5))
print("Test AUC evaluated in section 12  :", round(roc_auc_score(y_test, test_proba[best_name]), 5))
assert np.allclose(check_proba, test_proba[best_name], atol=1e-6), "Packaged pipeline does not reproduce the evaluated model!"
print("OK: identical predictions.")

























Test AUC of the packaged pipeline : 0.78661
Test AUC evaluated in section 12  : 0.78661
OK: identical predictions.





















In [59]:






# ---- Step 2: re-fit on ALL customers for the final model (more data = slightly better; the test score above is our honest estimate) ----
final_pipeline = build_deploy_pipeline().fit(df[RAW_FEATURES], y_all)

# ---- Step 3: save it (Parquet = what the app loads; joblib = the standard Python alternative) ----
Path("models").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
best_row = comparison.loc[best_name]
metadata = {
    "model_name": best_name,
    "target": "deposit = yes (the client subscribes to a term deposit)",
    "default_threshold": 0.5,
    "raw_features": RAW_FEATURES,
    "cv_roc_auc": float(best_row["cv_auc_mean"]),
    "test_roc_auc": float(best_row["test_roc_auc"]),
    "test_precision_at_0.5": float(best_row["test_precision"]),
    "test_recall_at_0.5": float(best_row["test_recall"]),
    "trained_on_rows": int(len(df)),
    "note": "Metrics come from the train/test evaluation in the notebook; the saved model was then re-fitted on all rows.",
    "library_versions": {lib.__name__: lib.__version__ for lib in (pd, np, sklearn, lightgbm, xgboost, shap)},
}
save_model_parquet(final_pipeline, "models/best_model.parquet", metadata)
joblib.dump(final_pipeline, "models/best_model.joblib")

# ---- Step 4: reload from the Parquet file and make sure nothing was lost in translation ----
reloaded, reloaded_meta = load_model_parquet("models/best_model.parquet")
sample = df[RAW_FEATURES].sample(500, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
assert np.allclose(final_pipeline.predict_proba(sample), reloaded.predict_proba(sample)), "Reloaded model differs!"
print("Reloaded model gives identical predictions on 500 clients.")
print({p.name: f"{p.stat().st_size / 1024:.0f} KB" for p in Path("models").iterdir()})
display(pd.read_parquet("models/best_model.parquet", columns=["model_name", "created_utc", "metadata_json"]))

The Streamlit app¶
The app (streamlit_app.py, next to this notebook) loads models/best_model.parquet and offers:


    

  • Single client — fill in a form and get the probability of subscribing, a "contact / don't prioritise" recommendation, and a SHAP explanation of that prediction.
    • 

  • Bulk upload — upload a CSV of clients, rank them, flag the prospective ones (by cut-off and/or by how many clients you can afford to contact), download the results, and inspect the SHAP explanation of any client plus the overall drivers.
    • 



To run it, open a terminal in this folder and type:


.venv\Scripts\streamlit run streamlit_app.py



(On macOS/Linux: .venv/bin/streamlit run streamlit_app.py.)






















16. Conclusions, limitations and next steps¶
What we achieved¶
    

  • Framed the problem around a real constraint — limited capacity to contact clients — and judged the model accordingly: ROC-AUC to select it, precision (share of contacted clients who subscribe) as the business KPI.
    • 

  • Profiled and cleaned the data: classified the hidden missing values (MCAR / MAR / MNAR / structural), removed 8 duplicate rows before splitting, tested normality (irrelevant for our models), checked multicollinearity with VIF (harmless for accuracy) and engineered 7 features.
    • 

  • Built a baseline ladder (majority class → best single-feature lookup) and 7 model types from logistic regression to Google's YDF, plus Optuna-tuned XGBoost and LightGBM, all with identical features, splits and cross-validation folds. The top models are statistically tied (test ROC-AUC ≈ 0.78–0.79 vs 0.68 for the best simple baseline).
    • 

  • Chose the best model with an explicit rule (one-standard-error rule, then least overfitting): LightGBM (Optuna) — test AUC 0.787, precision 0.80, recall 0.60 at the 0.5 cut-off.
    • 

  • Watched for over- and underfitting (train/CV/test gaps, learning and validation curves): no model is badly overfit, and the chosen model has the smallest gap (+0.028) among the tied models.
    • 

  • Explained the best model and YDF with permutation importance, SHAP and partial dependence.
    • 

  • Packaged the model: one pipeline from raw client record to probability, saved as models/best_model.parquet (plus .joblib) and served through a Streamlit app with single-client prediction, bulk upload and SHAP explanations.
    • 



What it means for the campaign¶
On the held-out test set (1 561 clients, 48 % of whom subscribe), using the best model:






Strategy

With the default cut-off, about 20 of every 100 contacts are wasted, versus 52 of every 100 when contacting at random. The team can trade volume for precision with the app's cut-off slider or by capping the number of clients to contact.


Limitations (please read)¶
    

  • Model ceiling. All strong models plateau around 0.78 AUC and are statistically tied; the chosen model is "best" mainly because it overfits least. Better features or more data would help more than more tuning.
    • 

  • month and campaign are recorded after the fact. campaign (number of contacts in this campaign) is only fully known once the campaign is over; month is the last contact month and may reflect which clients had already been selected. In the app, campaign should be read as "contacts made to this client so far". With no dates we cannot test either properly.
    • 

  • No dates, so no time-based validation. A random split can be optimistic when clients are correlated over time; the model should be re-validated on a later campaign before it is trusted.
    • 

  • contact = unknown depends on how contacts were logged (concentrated in May–June). If recording practice changes, the model's use of it will not carry over.
    • 

  • Single test split. Its margin of error is about ±0.015 AUC.
    • 

  • Fairness. The model uses age and job. Before using it to decide whom to contact, check it does not discriminate unfairly and comply with local regulations.
    • 

  • Correlation, not causation. SHAP and permutation importance explain what the model uses, not what would happen if the bank intervened.
    • 

  • Pickle security. The Parquet model file contains a Python pickle: only load model files you created yourself.
    • 



Next steps¶
    

  1. Obtain a date or campaign-wave column and validate forward in time; consider removing campaign for a model that must decide before any contact is made.
    2. 

  2. Add richer client features (tenure, number of products, transaction behaviour) — the biggest likely gain.
    3. 

  3. Turn the cut-off into a cost model with the bank's real cost per contact and value per deposit.
    4. 

  4. Monitor precision and calibration after deployment, and retrain when they drift.
    5. 

  5. Add a fairness review.
    6.
